blocks.x: It's my great pleasure to be here with one and only Alan Toussaint here on Clementa Street here at C. St. Studios. We'll go over some general questions about your past and the many musical things you've been involved in. First, did you have any formal training in piano?
As a child, a total of a couple of months, actually.
That's astounding. So you just took it up on your own? Oh, that's the piano that's concerned, yeah. Who would you cite as people that you'd like to listen to and as influences on your playing?
At that time or any time?
At that time particularly.

I liked all records, all the records that are out here. And I liked Ranky Tank type pianos. I liked Fats Waller. I liked Professor Longhair, of course. Ray Charles. Lloyd Glenn. Albert Hammond. By Albert Hammond. Fuck like that.
Did you go to, I think it was a green high school with James Rivers? I think you were like a year or two ahead of him. I think an Art Neville and James Black.

Not green school, I don't think. I registered for a green school one year. I think it was when it was, well, I don't know what was going on during that period, but it was some sort of transitional period going on. And I registered, but I didn't go to that school green. So I didn't get that. James Rivers and I went to Booker T together.

Were there a lot of other musicians that, well, a lot of other people who have gone on to be great New Orleans musicians there at the time, attracted by the marching band? A few, a few, I'd say, but not super, super lucky with me. Was one of your first gigs playing with Shirley and Lee on the road alternating with Huey Smith?

Not alternating with it. I took Huey's place. Huey's records had begun to do very well. So it was time for him to go on his own. I went to take his place, whether it would be temporarily or permanent, and it ended up in being permanent, the first trip. So we weren't alternating, actually.
What do you think of Huey's influence on New Orleans music?

Very strong and very authentic. He's one of the true bloods of it all. He's in the studio now recording, isn't he? Well, he was a couple of months ago. He's through with that particular project. Whether he's about to start another one, I don't know. But at present, he's not in.
You worked for a couple of years with Ace Records, if I'm not mistaken.

Yeah. I couldn't consider working with them because at that time, I was a sideman piano player, and I would play with whoever was going to be in that time. And if it so happened to have been Ace Records, I would play it. And if they came back in a couple of weeks, I'd play it again. But I couldn't consider that working with all four of Ace.

Well, as a sideman, were you in a better position than most of the other musicians? Because the people that worked for Ace seemed pretty bitter looking back. They said they were never paid. That they'd be promised this, that, and the other, and that they're just really never taken care of. Were you better treated back then?

I suppose I may have been better treated because there was no promises made, so none broke unto me. So I wasn't into the disappointment of promises. There just weren't any. And I was a sideman musician, and I'd play on a session, and I'd get the scale sometimes. Well, most of the time.
Even then, did you prefer to work in the studio as opposed to performing live?

No. Actually, back then, I considered myself a live sideman musician. A live musician, whether it be sideman or not. And recordings was something that was extra, as far as I was concerned. I liked recording a lot. I had a lot of respect for it. I knew it was closer to the world than live recording. I mean, than live performances. I knew that you could record one time, and they would hear it in England. But at that time, I was mostly a musician on stage.
Was that the time when you were working with Lee Allen a lot?
I worked with Lee Allen in the studio. Mm-hmm. So it's that period, yes. Mm-hmm. But as on stage, I didn't work with Lee Allen much. He was along with Paul Gaten and that group, Earl Palmer.
And so forth. How did you get involved in production work? Was that through Dave Bartholomew?

Well, I guess he may have been one of my early introducers to that field, but I didn't actually produce for Dave. I played the piano for Dave, and I may have assisted some, but Dave was actually the producer there. I actually got into production, I guess, with minute records first. I had been doing what was equivalent to that a few times before with others that came into the studio sometime. Someone would bring an artist through without material or anything and send him in and tell him to go to the piano player and see what y'all can get up. So I began doing that, but I didn't consider that being in the business. But I guess we held with minute records.
That was with Larry McKinley and Dave Bartholomew originally?
Joe Banaszczak. Joe Banaszczak. Joe Banaszczak, Larry McKinley.

Dave Bartholomew was with Imperial Records. And those artists that you first worked with on minute included like Lee Dorsey, Jesse Hill, Irma Thomas, Aaron Neville. Yeah. Just hit after hit, great. One classic, song after another. You wrote, did you write Oop Oop Oop Oop Oop?
No, Jesse Hill wrote that. I produced it and, well, at that time it was called A&R Man. So I did whatever they do and played, of course, played the piano on it, but I didn't write it. He wrote that.
And, yeah, yeah, did Lee Dorsey write that or did you write that? Lee Dorsey wrote that himself.
I assisted with the arrangement of that.

New Orleans, I think, in the 60s had a lot of novelty records that sewed really well. I guess they were called novelty then. And Huey Smith told me that he thought that the music and musical games that children play just on the streets really, he thinks that really has a big influence or did have a big influence on New Orleans music then. What do you feel about that?

Well, here I can certainly afford to speak of that because he was such a mess that those novelty type tunes. I can see a correlation there. There was a whole era of things like doing the Shirley Ellis days of Banana Banner for Fenn and things like that. And they had a lot of these and Purple People Eater even. So those that I consider novelty. I guess in the whole general sense, yes, they do have a lot to do with the street. A lot of novelty tunes that I've written that turned out to be novelty. I didn't associate with children's game, but I did associate it with some type of humor. I considered mother-in-law a novelty.

Okay. At that time, it seemed like almost all the New Orleans music that we know today was being written by you like It's Raining and Ruler of My Heart and Over You. Did you write those songs specifically with, okay, did you write It's Raining with Irma Thomas in mind or did she come to you and say, connect me up with something that I'll be able to sing well? How did that go? How did that go?

and songs like It's Rainin' the Root of My Heart, the artist was usually right there, and we'd write one tune, and sing it down once and the artist go, and in the next room in practice while we write another song for someone else. Then one come out of the other room, and we'd sing that, and then the other one would go in the other room. And whoever wasn't working on their own songs would sing background for the others. So when It's Rainin' was written, I'ma was there. For most of the songs she was right there, actually. She was a lot of inspiration, though, so many songs she weren't really around for because they were written in the car sometimes,
on the way between parts. So music just comes to you at all different times of the day, and it's something that never stops.
Right. Some trash and some real.
Why in the 60s did you write under the name Naomi Neville? Naomi Neville. Naomi.

That's my mother's maiden name. out in Tibidore and Shriburri pronounced it John Neville, which was my grandfather. I had, when mother-in-law was written and things before that, I was underage. And there were people that would come through town and collect a lot of things, masters, and they'd sell them out to different companies. And I was a product of that for a while. It's just not so terrible. It just was a way of doing things at that time. And I was out on a particular label, which was an alright label. But after that, there was no more affiliations actually, or things being done or even undone. And later, as I began to go into a business with others, it became a problem on whether that contract was still valid or void. So until they got that straight, I wrote under Naomi Neville. And it took a while, but for that period, I did write under Naomi Neville.
Who has all the old Minute material, like all the old tapes of that?

Minute was sold to Liberty Records. Not Liberty Act. Minute was sold to Imperial. That used to distribute Minute. Imperial, I think, was bought out by Liberty Records. Maybe Liberty was bought out by someone else. The company was Travis Music, a publishing company. And Post, that's how the statements would come. So they are the ones who actually have the legitimate titles to publish. And the songs. As far as tapes of a lot of those things, I probably have a seven and a half of a lot of them. They just got onto a stacking stadium in the comments.
Would you like to see some of that old material re-released? Not really.
If someone just wanted to do it for some nostalgic reason, it's alright. But it's like releasing an old car. And they were really good during their days, but doing that day...
You want to work on something new. Right.

There's just too much going on. Too many musical changes and instruments that have been developed that would outlaw a lot of things that used to happen. And so, I think that's why the electronics is so far ahead.
I guess since we're on advanced electronics, do you intend to try digital recording in the near future?
What facet of digital? What facet of digital? You might know more about that.

Uh, yes. Basically, all I've heard about it is the idea that a few limited records are being made, that are being recorded digitally, and the digital tape is being played through a computer and worked with, by computers working on the notes themselves, rather than electronically reverbing and altering the notes. Mm-hm. That the actual frequencies are being changed in the digital recording. I was wondering how difficult would that be to get into? Well, with things like that, that's in your schematic and the manual.

It doesn't sound very spiritual, so I don't guess it's a matter of, do you have the directions? Uh, the guy that comes with the instrument. I'm not quite sure what you mean, but if it's something super automated, uh, like extrapolation on the conventional synthesizer. Music is moving closer to electronics, but as far as me actually manipulating these other things that change frequencies and pitch, that's a whole nother job. Uh, and that's another job other than just being a musician or a songwriter who writes another song.

Uh, see the digital recording wouldn't be related to synthesizers or electronic instruments as much as it would be, uh, from what I've heard, they actually record onto the tape the frequency of the note that's being played. Oh, okay. And they can manipulate that frequency of the note as a digital number. And supposedly the recording is supposed to be very, very pure. Very pure sound, almost direct to this quality.

Oh, well, if it's any improvement for us quality-wise on what a person would hear, I guess electronically they may get to that. That doesn't faze me very much. If that becomes the end thing, the studio should have that. I should continue learning music and people, ETC, pure, pure, pure, pure. Things like that.

Two more questions, I think, from the old minute days. That's you doing the piano dirge on, uh, over you for, uh, that Aaron Neville released, isn't it? It's like a great little intro. Was that, uh, was that one of the first things you did with him? I've read, I've read all these conflicting things that that came out originally in 1960, but it wasn't released on an album till after to tell it like it is was?
Oh yeah, I guess so. Oh yeah, it was done very early in our recording days. Uh, yes. In fact, that and over you was the first thing we did. Yeah.

Was that released as a 45 originally? Yes, it was. In 1960. And a question about Certain Girl, which, uh, uh, I think Ernie Cato recorded with you. Was that, is that based on a New Orleans saying? Like, I can't, uh, let me see. There's a certain girl, uh, there's a certain girl real sweet on, uh, and then, you know, you know what the lyrics go like, and then, I can't tell you her name until I get her. Is that, is that like a, uh, is that just a saying here, or is that something you just came up with?

That part is not, uh, a saying here, I wouldn't say. That, uh, there's a certain girl I've been after a long, long time. What's her name? Can't tell you. No. That was, if there was anything that I thought should have been the hook line or anything, that would have been, what's her name? Can't tell you. No. And the way it was done, the shape of it, and the little voice saying no. I do think, what's her name? Can't tell you. No. Is New Orleans. To say something and then say no behind it. Or either say, you better do what I say. Yeah. To say yeah behind it. Or I can't tell you no. Things like that, yes. But, uh, can't tell you a name until I get her. No. Okay. That just fit.
And that song later went on to be a rather well known rock song by the Yardbirds, the middle 60s. On Mother-in-Law, did you have, did you have both Benny Spelman and Ernie Cato in that?

Right. That's an incredible combination. Well, Benny Spelman had the type of voice that could do that. That low part would need that. And it was Ernie Cato's record, actually. And the background voices was Calvin LeBlanc, Willie Harper, and Benny Spelman.
You had to leave minute records for the Army. What happened? Were you drafted in 1963?

Right. That must have really disrupted things. A bit, yes. I was, by that time I was ready to go to the Army. I had been deferred a couple of times before then. And one time I was out because my left foot was in a cast from putting on trampoline shows. I had an accident. But I had been deferred a couple of times. So by January of 63, I didn't mind going to Army. A lot of artists did leave and ventured to other places. Of course, it was a blessing for some, seemingly. The first actual million seller that Irma had wished someone would care. After all of our recording days, her first real million seller was someone would care. And that was when I was in Army.
And you just heard it on the radio while you were probably on the case.

On the late one time I heard it and I thought it was gorgeous. Also, Aaron's first actual million seller being tell it like it is was one that I didn't do. That was after the Army period, at least during the Army period.
And you were with a group called the Stokes and it was then that you put out, you wrote Whipped Cream, which was later covered by Herb Albert. Right. Right.

Right. Whipped Cream was written for the Stokes as a joke. We'd do things in the Stokes, even though it was supposed to be a conventional rock band. We would do things like Spike Jonze and we'd rehearse the tune sometime that we had to tear a piece of paper or drop a piece of tin on the floor. So we had lots of things that was in the order of Whipped Cream. Whipped Cream was one of them.
You had written Java a couple of years before, about five years before that, for yourself, hadn't you? And then that was picked up by All Herb.

Right. Right. Right. Actually, in the writing of Whipped Cream, one thing that did make Whipped Cream a bit unique from the other tunes right in that same year of instrumentals, I did have Al Hurt in mind after he had did Java. I hadn't thought of Java for a trumpet or anything. And Al Hurt did inspire a lot of songs. It's easier to write what Al Hurt in mind. You can write forever. It's like writing for Aaron Neville's Iron Man Thomas. You can write for them without stopping.
After you got out of the Army, didn't the All For One group get together with Harold and Batiste? Was that pretty soon after that?
After, after. Yeah. I don't know whether it was, I think it was a little before.
What was the philosophy behind AFO was to have like musicians produce themselves and control their distribution? What was the philosophy behind that? Behind what? Behind the AFO.

There were certain musicians making a lot of sessions and playing on a lot of hit records. And they thought they would form a corporation of mainly them, which was a very good idea. And I think that's what it was about. Just that they would reap some benefits of whatever success they could be responsible for. And they were fairly involved in that group? Very fairly for a little while. Not very much.
Okay. I think that's been overstated in several accounts I've read about you.

Well, we never, I never made any moves with them or got anything going on. I definitely agreed with them. And I was sort of like a member by proxy sort of. But never really got together with them. I did anything.
Do you think that idea was almost too advanced for a lot of musicians to work?
Oh no. Oh no. The idea of it was business and business is over. So I don't think it was too advanced.
Do you think it could be, it could be done today then? Oh yeah. Some people got together.

It could be done. It could be done. I don't know if it, if it would be for the best interests of people because being a good businessman is important and being a good musician is. And if you're going to really develop your instrument, I don't know how much you develop your business skills along with it. You can do both. But for a whole group of people, it would be over average of being fortunate to find eight or ten men who can play and will do business together, actual business on an equal level. That's just very hard.
You're about the only person locally I can think of who really does handle both a lot of business and a lot of music. Where do you prefer to spend your time?
With those two subjects there?
Yeah. Would you rather be at the piano most of the time than?

Oh yes. All the time. All the time. Right. I, I entered the business part just out of necessity. No love for the business at all. I understand it. I don't dislike it. I have a lot of respect for it and I believe that this business is, is as legit as any business around in any country. And I think it has reached a good standard. But still it's business and I'm a musician. That's how I really feel.
But this has given you much, much greater control over the way your music comes out than for a lot of other musicians. And more control of really destiny.

Destiny. Destiny. Destiny. Well, maybe some things do. But I think musicians can, can be involved with the way that things come out. But it's such a responsibility to tell. I don't know if that's a curse or a blessing. To be responsible for spending someone's $150,000 on what you thought was right. Mm-hm. Actually, I had been playing with Earl King and Roland Cook, who was the bass player for Earl King. And there was a guy named Danny Kessler coming through town to pick artists and to search for talent. And he was going to record a few artists, namely Roland Cook and Roy Gaines and maybe Tommy Ridgely or someone like that. And I was there to play the piano behind Roland Cook or Roy Gaines or whoever else might be there that day. And as we were laying things down, Danny Kessler heard me playing and he would say, turn the piano up. That was popular to say during that day for some reason. Turn the piano up. And when the session was over, he came to me and asked me, could I get anything ready to record? And I said, well, I'll give him a try. He came back, I guess, in a week or so and we did the album. And it was leased to RCA.

I don't think I've heard any tracks from that. Great. Great if you haven't. Something best left forgotten. Got some tape left on that. In 1965, if I'm not mistaken, we got together with Marshall Seahorn for Sansu Enterprises. And that's when you put out some great things about Lee Dorsey working in the coal mine. Holy Cow. Did those just come to you like driving in the car and things like that? Those are such, I think those kind of define the New Orleans fun song. Things that you always want to sing over and over again to yourself.

Lee Dorsey's way of being and his voice has a lot to do with those songs being in existence. None of the Lee Dorsey songs would have been written if it wasn't for Lee. I would say that. Well, in a way the same for Irma Thomas, but there are some songs that I wrote for Irma that sound quite normal to me as a normal song. But Lee Dorsey's songs were written where I wouldn't dare draw them on someone else.

Just as you have to have somebody who's fun to work with for songs like Holy Cow and working on a coal mine, do you think that for someone like Irma Thomas and for blues, to get that really real sound that somebody has to have had a certain amount of real pain in their life and be singing that out? Because you don't hear that in a lot of California white musicians today. It's just that they kind of hit rhythm and blues, but they miss something. I don't know if I have all of that question. Okay. Do you think just as it's important for somebody to put out a fun song, to actually have enjoyed it, do you think that for somebody to put out something like Irma Thomas, like Wish Someone Would Care, that they've got to have been there at some point in their life?
But to come across the way the song was designed to be, theoretically it sounds right that you should have been there.
You had to go through those feelings.

I do say theoretically because there's something about people that work hard at things that I can't overlook. And I've seen some little youngsters that hasn't been around long enough to have been through too much, and they sing with so much like Michael Jackson. I hear more feelings in him sometimes than an 80-year-old man.
That's amazing.

But in a case like in Irma, there's so much about Irma's life that is so earthy. The first thing about Irma is it's earthy. It's definitely earthy. Then now what? So I think the difference in, I would rather define it as being more earthy than that you have to have been in certain places to. I hope that makes some sort of sense.

It does. It does. And not too long after that, I think it was in the late 60s, you all put together the meters. Were the meters together before they came to you all or did you kind of connect them up?
No, they were together very much so. Odd Neville and the Neville sounds. Planet of the Ivanhoe. Great little band.
I hope that makes some sort of sense.

It does, it does. And not too long after that, I think it was in the late 60s, you all put together the meters. Were the meters together before they came to you all, or did you kind of connect them up?
No, they were together, very much so. Art Neville and the Neville Sound, playing at the Ivanhoe. A great little band. And that's how they came.
And the song that came out at that time, no, I'll wait a little bit on that. So then they came into the studio. Did you see them at that point as being a New Orleans answer to Booker T and the MGs?
Had never thought about Booker T. But I guess whatever Booker T means in his area, or meant in his area, yes.
You know that emphasis on the organ instrumentals, piano instrumentals.

Well, I thought of them as instrumental groups, so the most, it consists of only rhythm sections, so it's not too much variation from that. You could get and still have the meters. Whether the solo be organ, piano, or guitar.

In the 60s, New Orleans music declined in popularity as far as nationwide appeal. What do you think caused the inability of the independent record companies to function because of the high capital involved in putting out a record? Do you think it was heard by the invasion of English music?
What period?
In the middle 60s and late 60s. From your point of view, what happened then?
I don't know. Don't really know.

You recorded a second album, which I like a lot. I hope you feel good about it. It was on Tiffany Records, simply entitled Two Saints, with Mack Rebinack and Earl Turbington, to name but a few. And that was recently released on an English label, I think two years ago, and it finally came back to New Orleans. And we played it, playing it tremendously on WTUL this last summer. Do you have good feelings about that album? It has working on a coal mine on it and a lot of beautiful instrumental work.

I remember it. And that's the way it is. I remember it. I never hear it anymore, of course. I remember doing it and it felt very different from that much singing going on for the first time. On the earlier album, it was all instrumental. So I could hold on to the piano. But to sing, sing your spirit through a microphone. Steve Terrell, that was with Scepter and Juan Records, talked up that album. And I consented to do that, but I'd never tried that before.

I forget on which piece. I think it might have been on a thing called Pickle. You've had a little bit, a few piano bars from the beginning of the Hallelujah Chorus. Do you remember that? It's just this... That's a real nice surprise in that. Makes it a lot of fun. A song that's been a mystery to me, I didn't even discover until I was putting together another program, was something you, I think you wrote for Aaron Neville called Hercules. Did you write that and arrange it?
Right.
Right. Do you remember who's in the band on that?

I think that was on the session in Atlanta, that we did some in Atlanta and some here. And a couple of Atlanta musicians, not a couple more than that of Atlanta musicians, like Barry Bailey, I think, who's with Atlanta Rhythm Section now.
I think tone on bass.
I would have to go downstairs and look at that and take another look at that.
That's a song I really wish had gone further. Is that one that you thought would? Or it seemed like it was a song that should have gone a lot further than it did.

I don't know. When we were through with it, I listened and it... It sounded like an awful lot of words, but I sort of liked it. It was written especially for Aaron to do. If it wasn't for Aaron, a song like that wouldn't have been written. To say those things. There are a lot of lines in there as the kind of lines that Aaron rapped when he talked. He talked like that. And he inspires a lot of things. Not that that's a different story that I know of, but... I could easily set up a scene from Aaron talk and write songs like that all day long.

I played that song on a show we did with the Neville Brothers about two months ago. And I don't think it's possible to find a copy of that record anywhere in the city now. Because there's such a huge response to it. And when it came out, I never heard it here in New Orleans.

It didn't do much at all. And it was a different sounding record for us. It was a little more... It sounded like a little more percussion. A little more production also. But it didn't do very much, but we liked it.

We have another question pertaining to the Neville's. You wrote all these things for Art Neville. Right. Which, of course, did very well. And then did very well about two years ago covered in a country version. Did that surprise you when it came back up again?
Very much so. It came out of the woodwork.

Is there a story behind... Okay, there's Art Neville's version of that song and then Aaron Neville did one after that. Was that done right after he came out with Tell It Like It Is, capitalizing on his popularity then?
No, I think right off the toe like it is, they had a fling of things that they were doing with the same producers and so forth during that time. So this was a bit after that. Quite a bit after that.
Going into some more up-to-date things. When did you open the studio? Yeah. Maybe five years now.
We could be more accurate downstairs.
Was there any particular thing that prompted you to do it or did you just want to control your own sound and provide an outlet for local musicians?

The studio came about out of necessity. The other studio in town, and I would say at that time, the studio in town, wasn't quite keeping up to certain standards. I'm sure that even they would have liked themselves. It just wasn't quite up to date on a lot of things. Marshall and I decided that if we could pull it off to get one going. It was actually designed for us to do our own recordings here. Shortly after opening, we learned that you don't open the studio just to record yourself.
So you've had a working relationship with Marshall Seahorn for almost 15 years?
Well, I guess it could be it. It's legitimate. Ladder 65. 65.
What aspects does he handle here in the studio now? He's a go-getter.
Contracts coming in, going out. In voices, who holds, who...
A lot of the day-to-day business operations. Oh, yes.
The whole thing.

If you don't object, I'd like to ask you a couple things about how you run the studio. There seems, from what I hear, there's like some sort of different systems. If somebody wants to come in here, pay you for the time, the studio's open to them. You know, so... Bonnie Raitt's recorded here. Paul McCartney's been here. King Biscuit Boy. The Mighty Diamonds. Robert Palmer. And so that's one aspect of the studio. Like, the musician can come here and pay you for the sessions. And you produce... And you produce the sound. And then the other system seems to be... And this, I think, applies to a lot of local musicians, is that... Since most of them don't have a lot of money, they can come in here and record. And they don't pay you unless the record actually sells.

Unless it can be placed somewhere and they can be reimbursed. For instance, if there's a group and they're not with anyone, they can come in and make a demo session or just record a session. And the studio bill will be calculated, but not issued to them. Then if they want to take it somewhere and try to place it with the company, let someone hear it and see if someone accepts it, they can do that. And if they find someone that accepts it, who will give them fronts, you might call it, which is only to reimburse what they've paid. Then they could pay the studio bill. Or if the company would take it and not give them any fronts, well then we'd wait and if the record sells, then they would collect anything.
Get paid. Do you and Marshall try to find record labels for some of the local musicians?
Sometime, yes. When folks seek that service, yes.
So it seems like you have a very open philosophy about just trying to make the studio available for different people with different needs.
Through that you can find what various, if there's talent that can't afford to in other ways, you can always seek that out. At least hear it.

But some of the rock people have come in, what do you think has drawn them to New Orleans? Trying to get a New Orleans sound, just the city? Well, you have to be more specific about the particular person. Okay. There's somebody like Bonnie Raitt and Robert Palmer and the Mighty Diamonds. Three unique cases.
All right. Let's see.

We're discussing the reasons for, and I've just learned that they're really too diverse to lump them all together. Bonnie Raitt, the Mighty Diamonds, and Robert Palmer. Trying to find out what attracts them to the studio and what's made the studio really a musical center in the recording industry of the world.

Well, New Orleans, for one. And probably first. New Orleans. New Orleans. New Orleans 19, so and so. Just whoever's in existence at that time. And I do say New Orleans because we've been through Roy Browns, Bad Dominoes, etc. Lure Armstrongs, Al Hurts. So we've had giants in the world. And there's, it is a birthplace for a lot of things. So New Orleans is already attractive, the sound of it, the music. Bonnie Raitt is well-versed, I guess, if you know Bonnie Raitt at all. Yes, love her music. In all mundane and other music. So she wouldn't dare miss New Orleans in her scruples. She sometimes sounds like she was raised here, like she's lived here all for life. She loves it here. And I'm sure she loves other places that's sort of like this because there's some good areas around the country. And Bonnie Raitt's respect for the root music would keep her in touch with New Orleans and the likes.
